question: What is the meaning of material in relation to revision of the original design?
description: The term "material passport" refers to a digital model or dataset that describes the characteristics and quality of materials and components in products and systems. It aims to provide information that gives value for present use, recovery, and reuse. In the context of revision of the original design, a material passport can help identify materials that can be reused or recycled, potentially reducing waste and supporting sustainable design practices. This information can inform design decisions and contribute to the development of more circular and sustainable products.

years, a subgroup of applications originated referred as digital twins 
with aim to support sustainable or circular use of an object over its life 
cycle. These applications focus on the capability of a system to model 
future scenarios of the object (Barni et al., 2018). 
Some passports are addressed by terminology referring to a specific 
domain or task for which the passport is developed. For example, 
‘building passports‘ (Blum, 2009) and ‘building material passports” 
(Munaro et al., 2019) are specifically designed for registering informa­
tion on structures used for living or working and “digital battery pass­
ports” address those specifically for batteries (Bai et al., 2020). “Building 
renovation passports” emphasize also the task of assessing the quality 
state of a building and outlining options for renovation in its name 
(Fabbri et al., 2017a; Sesana and Salvalai, 2018). The term “cradle 2 
cradle passport”, although surprisingly once observed in the building 
industry (Futas et al., 2019), seems to be mostly associated with the 
MAERSK vessel project in which the role of the passport is to support 
decision making for ship deconstruction (Bendekovi´c et al., 2015; Ellen 
MacArthur Foundation, 2020; Sterling, 2011). The review of Debacker 
and Manshoven (2016) lists a number of other terms such as “workwear 
passport”, “circularity passport”, “resource identity tag”, and “technical 
passport for equipment”, that seem to originate as brand names from 
firms offering passports. Current regulation and legislation bodies of the 
EU have defaulted to naming convention “product passport” (G¨otz et al., 
2022). 
3.4. Definitions 
Many formal or informal definitions have been suggested for 
passport variants. Using the axial coding system we analyzed which 
features are used to compose each definition derived (Strauss and Cor­
bin, 1994) (see Table A4 (Appendix A2.2). We found there is overlap 
among a number of definitions but no unanimous agreement on the 
determinate features. This is no different among the equally termed 
passport variants. There also does not seem to be a growth of features 
over time nor a convergence toward certain features in composing 
definitions. The most frequently listed feature is ”the composition of 
components and materials of an object” followed by the primary pass­
port goal: ”the identification of reuse value in an object”. Remarkably, 
the second most mentioned goal of a passport in Fig. A3 (Appendix 3.1) 
was never found in a definition. Quite contrasting with the characteristic 
features resulting from the content analysis presented in Section 3.6 is 
the minor emphasis placed on two features, i.e., addressing it concerns a 
registration about a uniquely identifiable object, and that it concerns 
dynamic access to information on the life cycle history of that object. 
Other features can be naturally explained. For example, the emphasis 
placed on features such as disassembly guidelines and hazardous 
containment in the definition of Hesselbach et al. (2001) is reflecting the 
stringent focus of their passport variant on the recycling phase. The 
renovation roadmap feature included in e.g., Fabbri et al. (2017a) and 
Sesana and Salvalai (2018) may be something typical for building 
passports and building renovation passports. Some authors (Honic et al., 
2019a; 2019b) also rephrase an identified definition in their papers, 
reasonably to highlight specific parts or as an unintentionally result of 
different word use.
